claims.text: The applicable starting material is a single-phase solid-solution high-entropy alloy in which titanium and nickel are primary constituents.
Conventional slow cooling produces a relatively coarse grain structure in the proposed titanium- and nickel-based alloy.
Severe plastic deformation will significantly refine the alloy's grains.
The resulting grain structure will be nanometer-scale.
Short-duration, high-temperature flash annealing after severe plastic deformation will activate rapid recrystallization.
Flash annealing will minimize diffusion-driven grain growth.
The combined treatment will promote preferential segregation of titanium and nickel at grain boundaries.
Titanium and nickel segregation will pin and stabilize the grain boundaries.
Pinned grain boundaries will reduce grain-boundary sliding during high-temperature exposure.
Pinned grain boundaries will reduce microstructural coarsening during high-temperature exposure.
The proposed grain-boundary strengthening mechanism will enhance elevated-temperature microhardness.
The proposed grain-boundary strengthening mechanism will enhance elevated-temperature yield strength.
The treated alloy will have greater high-temperature tensile strength than the conventionally processed control.
The treated alloy will show a less pronounced hardness loss after prolonged thermal exposure than the conventionally processed control.
A conventionally processed baseline can undergo grain coarsening accompanied by a hardness decrease from approximately 1065 HV to 1000 HV during extended high-temperature annealing.
The proposed stabilization mechanism is applicable over approximately 700°C to 1000°C.
Minor alloying elements or impurities may alter the predicted grain-boundary stabilization mechanism.
The optimal deformation and flash-annealing parameters and the long-term thermal stability of the ultrafine structure remain uncertain.
